Consideration of the University of Rhode Island Total Budget Request for FY 2027, and recommendation for approval to the URI Board of Trustees.
Enclosure Abby Benson, Vice President, Administration and Finance Vice President Benson presented the Total Budget Request for FY27, noting that this request is brought to the Board annually.
Her presentation included comparisons to the FY26 enacted budget and the difference between the FY26 request and the FY26 enacted budget as a baseline for the FY27 request.
She noted that the enacted appropriation for FY26 was $115.3 Million (out of a total all-funds budget of $1.11 Billion).
For FY27, the appropriation request is $143.9 Million (out of a $1.16 Billion all-funds budget).
Details on the request can be found in the presentation linked here.

Vice President Benson discussed the assumptions for the development of the FY27 request, namely small increases in both undergraduate and graduate enrollment, a 3% across-the-board tuition increase (noting that the Board will officially approve any tuition change in February), and small increases to certain student fees (Fitness and Wellness Center Fee, Memorial Union Fee, and Building Fee).
She also noted challenges to enrollment including nearby state free/reduced tuition programs, the Hope and Promise scholarships in Rhode Island, the uncertainty of federal impacts on student aid, volatile interest rates, and the impact of the quality of URI housing on both recruitment efforts and yield.
Vice President Benson noted that the Current Service Level request includes funds for student aid, debt service, insurance rate increases, impacts to fringe benefit rates, and operating increases relative to new buildings on campus.

With reference to the Strategic Initiatives included in the request, Vice President Benson noted that this component included 10 new faculty members, 13 new Academic Advisors, and additional support for the Talent Development, National Guard, and Tribal Scholarship programs.
There are also funds for the development of a new merit scholarship, Anchor in Rhode Island, aimed at attracting the top students in the state, although development of this initiative is still ongoing.
In an additional slide, Vice President Benson showed how these requests align not only with the URI Strategic Plan, but also the State’s RI2030 Strategic Plan priorities.
Vice President Benson also discussed the state’s full-time equivalent (FTE) cap, noting that while student enrollment at URI has grown 19% over the last twenty years, the FTE cap has only increased 4%.
Responding to board member inquiry, Vice President Benson stated that URI is below its peers in terms of staffing in many of its support areas.
Board members encouraged continuing efforts to advocate to the state for an increase in the cap.

The Committee decided to vote on the FY27 Total Budget less the Anchor in Rhode Island scholarship, since it is still in development and may be discussed by the full Board at an upcoming meeting.
Chair Ownjazayeri called for a motion, and on a motion duly made by Armand Sabitoni, and seconded by Michael Fascitelli, it was VOTED: To recommend approval of the University’s FY2027 Total Budget Request, less the Anchor in Rhode Island scholarship, as presented in the enclosure.

MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS (Unaudited) - Continued (14) Using the Financial Statements The University’s financial statements are prepared in accordance with GASB principles, focusing on the institution as a whole rather than on individual funds or activities.
The University reports its operations as a business -type activity, utilizing the economic measurement focus and the full accrual basis of accounting.
This approach allows the University to recognize revenues when earned and expenses when incurred, providing a comprehensive view of its financial performance.
As a component unit of the Sta te of Rhode Island, the results of the University’s operations, net position, and cash flows are summarized in the State’s Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR).
This report is derived from the State’s government -wide financial statements, ensuring transparency and accountability in the University’s financial reporting within the broader context of state finances.
The University’s financial statements consist of three basic components: 1.

Statement of Net Position: This statement presents information on all of the University’s assets, deferred outflows of resources, liabilities, and deferred inflows of resources, along with the resulting net financial position.
Over time, changes in net position can indicate whether the University’s financial health is improving or deteriorating. 2.
Statement of Revenues and Expenses and Changes in Net Position : This statement details how the University’s net position changed during the most recent fiscal year.
It reports all changes in net position as soon as the events giving rise to those changes occur, regardless of when cash flows will actually take place.
T his means that revenues and expenses are recognized for items that may result in cash flows in future fiscal periods, such as payments for accrued compensated absences or amounts owed by studen ts for services rendered. 3.
Statement of Cash Flows: This statement is prepared using the direct method, which highlights net cash flows from operations as major classes of operating receipts (such as tuition and fees) and disbursements (like cash paid to employees for services).

These statements together provide a comprehensive overview of the University’s financial position, performance, and cash flows.
The financial statements can be found on pages 20 to 24 of this report.
The notes to the financial statements provide additional information essential to a full understanding of the data provided in the financial statements.
They also provide information regarding both the accounting policies and procedures the University has adopted as well as additional detail of certain amounts contained in the financial statements.

Compensated absences represent accumulated vacation, sick leave, and deferred compensation that will be used or paid in future years.

Investments in Capital Assets The largest portion of the University’s net position , $664.70 million and $598.92 million, as of June 30, 2025, and 2024, respectively, reflects its investment in capital assets (such as land, buildings, machinery, and equipment), net o f any related outstanding debts used to acquire, construct, improve, or rehabilitate those assets.
This represents approximately 86% for fiscal year 2025 and 85% for fiscal year 2024 of net position.
These capital assets are essential for providing services to students, faculty, and administration, and therefore, are not available for future spending.
While the University’s investment in capital assets is reported net of related debt, it is important to note that the resources required to repay this debt must come from other sources, as the capital assets themselves cannot be liquidated to settle the debt .
